tagline.text: Tour the Philippines' only nuclear plant, never once switched on

location.label: Location
location.text: Napot Point, Nagbalayong, Morong, Bataan, on the South China Sea coast

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱700–1,500 (day trip from Manila including round-trip transport, per person)

children.text: The Bataan Nuclear Power Plant, begun in the 1970s and completed in 1984, was the first nuclear plant in the Philippines. It was never fueled and has been kept in preservation ever since. With advance booking you can walk into the reactor building and the control room, which makes it a rare industrial heritage tour.
The Bataan Nuclear Power Plant (BNPP) stands on Napot Point in Morong, Bataan, about 100 km west of Manila. It was built on a coastal site facing the South China Sea, roughly

above sea level. It was the Philippines' first nuclear plant, pursued after the 1970s oil shocks to gain energy independence, and Westinghouse was the main contractor. Sources give its output as 620–623 MW, and a single pressurized water reactor (PWR) was built.

What makes the plant famous is that it was "finished but never run." Construction began in the mid-1970s and reached completion around 1984. A mix of safety reviews after the 1979 Three Mile Island accident, the 1986 Chernobyl disaster and change of government, and concerns about nearby fault lines and Mount Pinatubo meant no fuel was ever loaded, and in 1986 the plant went into preservation. Its construction cost is reported at about US$2.2–2.3 billion, and one source says the foreign debt was fully repaid in 2007. The state-owned National Power Corporation (NPC) still looks after it, so the equipment remains in remarkably good condition.

Since 2011 the plant has offered tours for students and the general public. Visitors hear an energy briefing, pass through the steam generator building, corridors and an airlock, climb to a deck inside the reactor building to look down on the reactor, and finish in the main control room, whose walls are covered with switches and gauges. According to the guides, fuel was never brought in, so there is no radiation risk, and the control rods are still in their original packaging. Whatever your view on nuclear power, it is a chance to see a country's energy policy and political history with your own eyes.

It is not a sightseeing spot you can simply walk into. Security is strict, advance booking and coordination are required, and walk-ins are not accepted. Weekday office hours are the norm. Rules, fees and whether tours are running can change as the debate over reviving the plant continues, so check the latest information before you go.

This is one of the first stops on the tour, a hall full of large machines, piping, knobs and switches that were never used. Decades of preservation work keep the equipment clean. Photography is reportedly allowed for personal use only, so avoid commercial use.
The reactor building is enclosed by concrete walls about
1 m

thick. After passing through a sealed airlock and a decontamination chamber, you climb steep stairs to a deck overlooking the reactor. There is no elevator and you must climb several flights, so you need some stamina and comfortable shoes.

blocks.title: Reactor deck and packaged control rods

children.text: From the deck you can see the top of the reactor and the control rods. Guides say uranium fuel was never brought in, and the control rods are still in the plastic wrapping they arrived in. It is the scene that best conveys the story of a plant that never ran.

The control room, with switches and panels covering entire walls, is described as looking just as it did around 1985. One visitor reported that the central telephone was a direct line to Malacañang Palace and that the president's go-ahead was needed to switch the reactor on or off. You can sense how closely politics and technology were intertwined during construction.

Tours usually begin with an introduction that presents nuclear power as an alternative energy source, a short history of the plant, and an explanation of the main facilities. Opinion on this plant is sharply divided, so it helps to listen knowing that the briefing is one side of a debate rather than taking it at face value.

Some records say about 15,000 Filipino engineers and workers built it, with hundreds of foreign technicians taking part. The Three Mile Island accident, Chernobyl, the 1986 change of government and fault-line concerns are often cited as reasons it stopped. Long-standing allegations of corruption are also part of the plant's story.

blocks.title: A site in the revival debate

children.text: In 2022 the Philippine president mentioned resuming nuclear research, and in October 2024 the Department of Energy was reported to have agreed with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power on a feasibility study for rehabilitation. Estimates of the restoration cost vary widely, from about US$1 billion in a 2010 evaluation to US$3–4 billion in Russia's Rosatom assessment of 2017. Watching what happens next is part of what makes a visit interesting.
Take a bus bound for Balanga from the Cubao bus station in Quezon City or the EDSA terminal in Pasay. Your tour booking and entry time must already be confirmed before you leave.
Arrive in Balanga city and have breakfast. Transfer to a bus or vehicle bound for Morong and head toward the west coast.
Arrive in the Nagbalayong area of Morong and complete the security check and registration. Bring your ID.
Attend the briefing, then be guided through the steam generator building, airlock, decontamination chamber, reactor deck and control room, in that order.
After the tour, have lunch. There are few good places to eat nearby, so it is safer to eat in Balanga or Morong town.
Stop at the nearby Pawikan Conservation Center (Nagbalayong beach) to see the sea turtle protection work, then head back.
Tour times are set by the plant's schedule, so the times above are only an example. Confirm the exact arrival time and duration when you book.

items.subtitle: Combine the plant with coastal villages

children.text: Start from the Subic or Olongapo side, or head west from Balanga. Having your own vehicle makes the trip much easier.
Arrive at the plant and begin your tour at the booked time.
Have lunch in a nearby beach village.
See the turtle egg hatchery and the small exhibit at the Pawikan Conservation Center.
Return along the Morong coastal road.
The Subic Bay Freeport and Morong are close, so they are easy to combine in one day, but travel times can vary greatly with road conditions.

Morong is about
51 km
from Balanga and about
175 km
from Manila by road. Using public transport alone takes a long time.
The usual way is to take SCTEX into Bataan and use the west coast road. Check road conditions and any roadworks before you leave.
The plant is in a remote spot and the last stretch is awkward by public transport. A private car or chartered vehicle is recommended.
Visitors report that part of the road into Nagbalayong is sandy and ordinary cars can get stuck.
You can also reach the plant from the Subic Bay Freeport side, coming down toward Anvaya Cove.
Traveling from Olongapo may feel shorter than coming from Manila.
Tour requests go through the responsible department of the National Power Corporation (NPC) or the Bataan tourism office. Contact details change often, so confirm through official channels.
Because the tour is mostly indoors, whether you can book matters more than the season. Still, it is hot and humid inside the buildings, so the cooler dry season is far more comfortable.

November to May has little rain and travel is easy. From March to May daytime temperatures are high and the buildings feel especially muggy, so bring plenty of water. In the June–October rainy season, rain and typhoons can affect roads and tour schedules.
Weekday office hours are the norm. For a weekend tour, there is a notice that staff overtime costs are added.

There are few large places to stay near the site, so most people make a day trip or stay in Balanga. Visitors report that places in Balanga such as The Plaza Hotel Balanga can help coordinate a visit. Small bungalows and resorts exist in the coastal villages, so check locally.

Eating in Balanga city is the safest choice. Arcee's Restaurant in Balanga comes up often in visitor reports as a long-known place. In the Morong coastal villages there are small restaurants serving grilled fish and Filipino home cooking.
Be sure to book in advance and get your tour date and time in writing or by text message.
Bring photo ID and cooperate with the security check.
It is very hot and humid inside. You need breathable clothing and sturdy shoes for climbing stairs.
Visitors report that photography is allowed for personal use only. Get separate permission for commercial filming.
Visitors report that bookings are easier to arrange for larger groups, so it is a good idea to gather a group.
Do not wander around without a guide. Move only along the set route.
The travel distance for a day trip is long, so leave early in the morning.
This is a divisive topic, so comparing the briefing with other sources helps you understand it.

Tours are by reservation, and rules, fees and whether they are allowed change from time to time. The fees and contacts here are based on past sources, so be sure to confirm the latest information with the NPC or the Bataan tourism office before you visit.
Do not approach the grounds or fences without permission. It is a high-security facility.
There is no elevator and the stairs are steep. Think carefully if you have bad knees or are traveling with young children.
Inside the buildings it is hot and poorly ventilated. If you feel dizzy, tell your guide right away.
Part of the road is sandy, so be careful if your car sits low.
Discussion about reviving the plant is active, so access rules nearby may change suddenly.
Heading north from the plant, you reach the Subic Bay Freeport area. It is a good place for the sea, forest and marine activities.
A war memorial shrine in Bataan where you can continue the story of the Bataan Peninsula's history.
The provincial capital of Bataan, with lodging and restaurants, makes a good base before and after the tour.
It protects sea turtles on the same Nagbalayong coast and is easy to combine with the plant tour.
